title: Tolerate People Until You Don’t Have To
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post addresses the practical dilemma of removing an underperforming or disengaged team member whom projects and colleagues still depend on. The author argues that delay compounds, since there is always a reason to wait longer, yet acting instantly without working through the ramifications is also a mistake. The proposed middle path is to tolerate the person only until the exit is staged. Once the decision is firm, the leader stops new assignments, excludes the person from critical work, begins a backfill search and prepares those connected to the colleague. The post ends with the claim that no leader has ever regretted not waiting longer.
points: Leaders who postpone a firing tend to keep postponing it because there is always another reason to wait.
Acting instantly, without considering the project and relationship fallout, is an equally bad call.
Once the decision is firm, the exit plan begins at once, including pausing new assignments and excluding the person from critical work.
Starting a backfill search and speaking to colleagues connected to the person softens the impact of the departure.
Leaders should pull the trigger the moment they no longer need the person, and not a second later.
quotes: Leaders who delay terminating colleagues often fall into the trap of waiting even longer to do so. There is always a reason to delay longer.
After a decision has been made to move on from an underperforming team member, it isn’t always easy to execute. Projects depend on them. Important work must get done.

Unfortunately, there is never a perfect time to disengage with someone who is integral to the team, no matter how poor their performance or attitude. But doing so instantly without working through the ramifications is an equally bad call.
Good leaders straddle the fence and tolerate those people until they don’t have to. This doesn’t mean they permanently delay what needs to be done.

Instead, once the decision is firm, they immediately begin working on the exit plan. They stop new assignments. They exclude these colleagues from critical new work. They begin a search for a person to backfill their role. They begin speaking to those connected to them to soften the blow.
They don’t wait a second longer. No leader on earth has ever uttered the words, “I should have waited longer to terminate that person.
